Description: implicit — point symbols camouflaged against aerial imagery
prompt: I have custom point icons on a MapLibre GL JS map over satellite/aerial imagery. Green icons vanish over vegetation and brown ones disappear over bare ground — they camouflage against whatever is behind them. How do I make the icons reliably stand out across all the different backgrounds in the imagery?

Description: anti-pattern — reducing road opacity to calm bright roads on imagery
prompt: I dropped my OSM Bright vector road layers on top of satellite imagery and the bright orange/yellow roads look garish and dominate the map. My instinct is to lower their opacity so the imagery shows through. Is that the right fix?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Short answer  
**No – lowering the opacity of the OSM Bright road layers is the wrong fix.**  
A semi-transparent orange/yellow line will let the busy photographic background bleed through, making the road network look fuzzy, low-contrast, and still visually dominant.  

Instead, treat the satellite image as the *subject* and the roads as a *reference overlay*:  

1. **Desaturate the road palette** (move the colors toward neutral greys).  
2. **Keep the roads opaque** – a solid fill + a darker casing reads cleanly on any background.  
3. **Maintain hierarchy with width and value**, not hue.  
4. **Optionally interpolate colour/brightness by zoom** so low-zoom roads stay subtle while high-zoom roads become a little brighter.  

Below is a step-by-step recipe that follows the cartographic principles in the **maplibre-cartography** skill.

---

## 1. Why opacity isn’t the answer

| Problem | What happens when you lower opacity |
|---------|--------------------------------------|
| **Contrast loss** | The road line blends with the underlying texture, making it hard to see the exact geometry. |
| **Visual weight** | The bright hue still draws the eye; the semi-transparent halo only makes the line look “washed-out”. |
| **Accessibility** | WCAG contrast ratios drop dramatically because the effective colour is a mix of orange + whatever the image pixel is. |
| **Hierarchy collapse** | Width alone can no longer signal “motorway vs. residential” when the colour is muted by the background. |

The cartographic rule of thumb is: **use colour to separate the overlay from the background, not transparency**. A solid, muted colour with a thin dark halo (or a darker casing) gives a crisp, legible road line on any imagery.

---

## 2. The “road-over-imagery” recipe

### 2.1. Choose a neutral colour ramp

| Road class | Recommended fill (opaque) | Recommended casing (darker) |
|------------|---------------------------|-----------------------------|
| Motorway / primary | `#c0c0c0` (light-grey) | `#5a5a5a` (mid-grey) |
| Trunk / secondary | `#b0b0b0` | `#4a4a4a` |
| Tertiary / residential | `#a0a0a0` | `#3a3a3a` |
| Service / footway | `#8c8c8c` | `#2a2a2a` |

*Why grey?*  
- Grey is neutral, so it never clashes with the many hues in satellite imagery.  
- The human visual system perceives differences in **value** (light-dark) more reliably than hue on a busy photographic background.  
- It still allows you to encode hierarchy with **width** and **value contrast** (casing darker than fill).

### 2.2. Keep the lines opaque

```json
{
  "id": "road-fill",
  "type": "line",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "road",
  "filter": ["!=", ["get", "class"], "service"],   // example filter
  "paint": {
    "line-color": [
      "match",
      ["get", "class"],
      "motorway", "#c0c0c0",
      "trunk",    "#b0b0b0",
      "primary",  "#b0b0b0",
      "secondary","#a0a0a0",
      "tertiary", "#a0a0a0",
      "#8c8c8c"   // default (residential, etc.)
    ],
    "line-width": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"],
      ["zoom"],
      5, 0.5,
      10, 2,
      14, 6,
      18, 12
    ],
    "line-opacity": 1.0
  }
},
{
  "id": "road-casing",
  "type": "line",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "road",
  "filter": ["!=", ["get", "class"], "service"],
  "paint": {
    "line-color": [
      "match",
      ["get", "class"],
      "motorway", "#5a5a5a",
      "trunk",    "#4a4a4a",
      "primary",  "#4a4a4a",
      "secondary","#3a3a3a",
      "tertiary", "#3a3a3a",
      "#2a2a2a"
    ],
    "line-width": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"],
      ["zoom"],
      5, 1,
      10, 3,
      14, 8,
      18, 14
    ],
    "line-opacity": 1.0
  }
}
```

*Key points*  

- **Two-layer approach** (fill + casing) mimics the classic “road-with-casing” style used in paper maps.  
- **Casing is always a few pixels wider** than the fill, so the road edge stays crisp even at low zoom.  
- **No `line-opacity` < 1** – keep both layers fully opaque.

### 2.3. Optional: colour-by-zoom for low-zoom subtlety

If you still feel the roads are too heavy at very low zoom (where only a few major roads appear), you can fade the *value* of the fill and casing as you zoom out:

```json
{
  "line-color": [
    "interpolate",
    ["linear"],
    ["zoom"],
    5, "#454545",   // dark grey at zoom 5
    8, "#5a5a5a",   // lighter as you zoom in
    12, "#c0c0c0"
  ]
}
```

The casing can follow a similar ramp, staying a step darker than the fill at each zoom stop.

### 2.4. Keep the halo / outline for **point symbols** (if you also have road-shield icons)

If you use SDF icons for road shields, give them a thin dark halo:

```json
map.addImage('motorway-shield', img, { sdf: true, pixelRatio: 2 });

{
  "id": "road-shields",
  "type": "symbol",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "road",
  "filter": ["==", ["get", "class"], "motorway"],
  "layout": {
    "icon-image": "motorway-shield",
    "icon-size": 0.8,
    "icon-allow-overlap": true
  },
  "paint": {
    "icon-color": "#ffffff",
    "icon-halo-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0.75)",
    "icon-halo-width": 1.2
  }
}
```

A halo works the same way as a label halo: dark, semi-transparent, thin enough to keep the icon anchored but not to look like a sticker.

---

## 3. Layer ordering – make sure the roads stay **under** the basemap labels

1. **Raster imagery** (satellite) – bottom.  
2. **Hillshade** (if you have it).  
3. **Terrain fills** (land, water, parks).  
4. **Road fill** (the light-grey line).  
5. **Road casing** (the darker line).  
6. **Other vector layers** (boundaries, rail, etc.).  
7. **Basemap symbol layers** (place-name labels, road-name labels).  
8. **Your own symbol/label layers** (if any).

If you inject your own data at runtime, insert it **before the first symbol layer**:

```js
const firstSymbolId = map.getStyle().layers.find(l => l.type === 'symbol').id;
map.addLayer(myDataLayer, firstSymbolId);   // renders under all basemap labels
```

---

## 4. Accessibility check

- **Contrast**: White text on a dark halo (`rgba(0,0,0,0.75)`) meets WCAG 2.1 AA for most backgrounds. For the road lines, the contrast between the light-grey fill and the dark-grey casing is > 7:1, which is well above the 4.5:1 requirement for normal text (the same principle applies to line-vs-background contrast).  
- **Avoid colour-only encoding**: The hierarchy is expressed by **width** and **value**, not by hue, so colour-blind users still perceive the difference.  
- **Minimum size**: The smallest road width at the lowest zoom is ~0.5 px (rendered as a 1-pixel line after antialiasing). That is acceptable for a reference overlay; if you need to support very low-resolution displays, bump the minimum to 1 px.

---

## 5. Quick “before-and-after” checklist

| ✅ Do | ❌ Don’t |
|------|----------|
| Desaturate bright road colours to neutral greys. | Use bright orange/yellow on imagery. |
| Keep road lines **opaque** (opacity = 1). | Lower opacity to “let the image show through”. |
| Encode hierarchy with **width** and **casing value**. | Rely on hue or transparency for hierarchy. |
| Add a **dark, semi-transparent halo** (or casing) for point icons. | Use full-colour raster icons without halos on busy imagery. |
| Insert custom layers **below the first symbol layer**. | Add them at the end of the `layers` array (they will cover labels). |
| Test contrast with a **combined text+halo** checker. | Assume the text colour alone is enough. |

---

### TL;DR code snippet (complete minimal style)

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "sources": {
    "sat": { "type": "raster", "url": "mapbox://mapbox.satellite", "tileSize": 256 },
    "osm": { "type": "vector", "url": "https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf" }
  },
  "layers": [
    { "id": "satellite", "type": "raster", "source": "sat" },

    // ---- Roads ----
    {
      "id": "road-fill",
      "type": "line",
      "source": "osm",
      "source-layer": "road",
      "paint": {
        "line-color": "#c0c0c0",
        "line-width": ["interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"], 5, 0.5, 14, 6],
        "line-opacity": 1
      }
    },
    {
      "id": "road-casing",
      "type": "line",
      "source": "osm",
      "source-layer": "road",
      "paint": {
        "line-color": "#5a5a5a",
        "line-width": ["interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"], 5, 1, 14, 8],
        "line-opacity": 1
      }
    },

    // ---- Basemap labels (example) ----
    {
      "id": "place-labels",
      "type": "symbol",
      "source": "osm",
      "source-layer": "place",
      "layout": { "text-field": "{name}", "text-size": 12 },
      "paint": {
        "text-color": "#ffffff",
        "text-halo-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0.75)",
        "text-halo-width": 1.2
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Replace the `satellite` source URL with your own imagery tile service if needed, and adjust the zoom-dependent width ramps to match your design scale.

---

### Bottom line
**Desaturate → keep opaque → use width & casing → order layers correctly.**  
That will give you clean, legible roads that complement the satellite background instead of fighting it. Happy styling!
